How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited (currently, a warning is provided regardless of whether the replication/reproduction study is already cited).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

When people are asked about philosophical thought experiments, the result is usually that different people give different responses. A question arises as to whether this variance is primarily a matter of differences between different people (between-person variance) or primarily a matter of each individual person giving different answers on different occasions (within-person variance). We disentangle these two sources of variance by administering five different thought experiments to participants and then giving them the same thought experiments again two weeks later. Across the five thought experiments, 66% to 79% of people gave the same answer both times. Using the intraclass correlation, we can compute the proportion of person-variance vs. within-person variance. Across the thought experiments, 25% to 52% of the total variance was between-person variance. Overall, these results indicate that a substantial proportion of the variance in responses to philosophical experiments is due to stable individual differences. Further research can explore which specific individual differences account for the between-subject variance and which specific cognitive processes account for the within-subject variance, but although the present study does not address those questions, it does provide an estimate of the total proportion of variance due to each of these sources.

[div-01]

Since the earliest day of experimental philosophy research, one of the most salient findings has been the high levels of variance observed in people's responses. When a sample of participants are all given the very same philosophical thought experiment, the result is often that some of them give one answer and others give the exact opposite answer. Much of the existing theoretical work in experimental philosophy has been devoted to explaining this variance. Such work aims to understand what it is that draws some participants to one answer and what it is that draws other participants to the opposite answer (see, e.g., Everett et al., 2021; Feltz & Cokely, 2024; Greene et al., 2001; Machery et al., 2004; Murray & Nahmias, 2014).

In this paper, we take up a question about the nature of the variance observed in these cases. One possible answer would be that it is primarily a matter of stable individual differences.

That is, it might be that there is some difference between participants such that some of them show a stable tendency to give one answer and others show a stable tendency to give the opposite answer. For example, it could be that when participants are asked which ship is the Ship of Theseus, some participants consistently answer that it is the ship made out of the replacement parts, while some consistently answer that it is the ship made out of the original parts.

Another possibility would be that it is primarily a matter of within-person variance. On this second view, the phenomenon is not primarily about different people being different from each other; it is primarily about each individual person having a certain probability of giving one answer and a certain probability of giving the opposite answer. For example, it could be that each individual person has a certain probability of saying that the ship made out of the replacement parts is the Ship of Theseus and a certain probability of saying that the ship made out of the original parts is the Ship of Theseus. If you give this same question to the same people two weeks later, those people might give different responses.

Of course, it will almost certainly turn out that what we are observing here is partly a matter of stable individual differences and partly a matter of within-person variance, but still, we face a question about the proportion of the total variance that arises from each of these sources. It could be that stable individual differences explain the vast majority of the variance and only a small proportion is within-person variance. Or it could be the opposite: perhaps the vast majority is within-person variance, and only a small proportion is explained by stable individual differences. The present study was designed to provide new data that bear on this question.

It seems plausible that the results of the present study might have important implications for distinctively philosophical questions. In the General Discussion, we turn to this issue, and we canvas a number of different views one might hold about the philosophical implications of these results. However, we will not be defending a specific philosophical view in this paper. Our aim is just to provide evidence regarding the empirical question. Of all the variance in judgments about philosophical thought experiments, what proportion is between-persons variance, and what proportion is within-persons variance?

Individual differences and conflicting intuitions

Thus far, existing work has not explicitly taken up the question as to what percentage of the variance in philosophical judgments is between-person vs. within-person, but some existing results do seem to bear on this question. There are suggestive findings on both sides.

On one side, there are studies that identify specific individual difference variables that influence people's intuitions. Men are more likely to make utilitarian judgments about trolley problems than women (Friesdorf et al., 2015), people who are higher in openness to experience are more likely to endorse moral relativism (Feltz & Cokely, 2008), those who have a more cognitive reflective style are likely to make incompatibilist judgments about free will (Hannikainen et al., 2019). These findings all suggest that at least some percentage of the variance in philosophical judgments is due to stable individual differences.

Within existing work, there is a complex ongoing debate about individual differences in judgments about philosophical thought experiments, but this debate has focused just on one particular type of individual difference. Specifically, the debate is about the influence of demographic factors, such as gender, culture and age (for opposing perspectives, see Alexander & Weinberg, 2025; Knobe, 2021; Stich & Machery, 2023). However, though there is ongoing disagreement about the extent and importance of demographic effects, both sides agree that at least some judgments show some effect of demographic factors, and all of the examples given in the previous paragraph are uncontroversial. More importantly, there is no debate about the importance of other individual difference variables, such as differences in personality and cognitive style. Studies consistently show that these variables do make a difference (Feltz & Cokely, 2008; Hannikainen et al., 2019; Machery et al., 2017; for a review, see Feltz & Cokely, 2024).

Much of this existing work is concerned with uncovering specific individual difference variables that impact judgments about philosophical thought experiments and looking in depth at those specific effects. For example, if there are effects of individual differences in judgments of free will, are those effects a matter of demographic differences, personality differences, or differences in philosophical education? By contrast, the present inquiry will not aim at identifying and exploring specific individual difference variables but rather at quantifying the total impact of individual differences as compared with other sources of variance. This is a separate but complementary task.

One way to think about the relationship between the two is that existing findings put a lower bound on the total percentage of variance explained by stable individual difference variables. To give just one example, there is a gender difference in judgments about brain-in-avat skepticism (Adleberg et al., 2015; Buckwalter & Stich, 2014; DeRose, 2017). This gender difference explains approximately 6.7% of the variance in brain-in-vat judgments (Adleberg et al., 2015). Thus, the total percentage of variance explained by all stable individual difference factors put together has to be at least 6.7%. But this still leaves a lot of uncertainty. For all we know, the total percentage of variance explained by all stable individual difference factors could be very low, very high or anywhere in the middle.

On the other side, there is some evidence that suggests that within-person variance might play an important role. A series of recent studies find that participants sometimes have intuitions pulling them in conflicting directions (Dranseika, 2024; Fischer et al., 2026; Knobe, 2026). In other words, it is not always the case that some participants have an intuition that p and others have an intuition that not-p; sometimes individual people have an intuition that p and also an intuition that not-p. In one study, participants were given philosophical thought experiments, asked to select the answer they thought was correct, and then asked whether they also felt an intuition pulling them to the opposite answer (Hannikainen & Knobe, 2026). For many questions, participants reported having conflicting intuitions. For example, of all participants who said that they did not know that they were not a brain in a vat, 81% reported that they also had an intuition pulling them in the opposite direction. This type of result suggests a certain picture of how people arrive at judgments in experiments like this one. Perhaps people initially feel pulled in two competing directions, then go through some further process in which they choose one of the two answers over the other.

To connect the idea of conflicting intuitions with the topic of the present paper, we need to introduce an auxiliary assumption. This assumption is that people who have conflicting intuitions will show greater within-person variance. To illustrate, imagine two different people who get the brain-in-a-vat question and give the skeptical answer. Now suppose that they differ when it comes to the internal psychological processes that led up to this answer. The first person only has skeptical intuitions, whereas the second person experiences a conflict between skeptical and non-skeptical intuitions and then ultimately chooses the skeptical answer. The basic idea of the auxiliary assumption is that this difference in internal psychological processes will be associated with a difference in within-person variance. The person who experienced a conflict between opposing intuitions will be more likely to switch her answers around if she is asked the same question on multiple different occasions. As far as we know, there are no studies that have explicitly tested this assumption, but it does seem plausible at a theoretical level. Moreover, it fits well with a larger picture within cognitive science, according to which judgments in these types of cases can be seen as samples from an internal probability distribution (see, e.g., Vul et al., 2014).

If we do make this assumption, we will be positing a link between the existing literature on conflicting intuitions and the topic of the present research. We might then conclude that the fact that people seem often to have conflicting intuitions gives us at least some initial reason to expect that there will be a substantial amount of within-person variance. But of course, all of this constitutes only very weak evidence. Even if a person has conflicting intuitions, it might be that one of the intuitions is stronger than the other. So if a person has conflicting intuitions, it could still be the case that she will very consistently choose one answer over the other. Alternatively, if a person uses a process of reasoning to choose between her conflicting intuitions, there might be stable individual differences in the operation of this reasoning process, which might lead some people to consistently choose one answer and others to consistently choose the opposite answer.

So the evidence that people have conflicting intuitions does not show just by itself that we will not find between-person variance in people's final judgments. Overall, then, existing evidence is inconclusive and points in opposing directions. The issue remains very much open.

The present study

In the present study, we give participants a battery of five philosophical thought experiments, then give those same participants the same thought experiments again after a two week gap. This method allows us to partition the variance in people's responses. The basic logic behind this approach is that if a large portion of the variance is due to stable individual differences, we will see a strong correlation between responses at two different times.

By contrast, if most of the variance is within-person variance, we would expect to find a relatively small correlation between responses at the two times.

This same technique has been applied in various other areas of psychology, unrelated to responses to philosophical thought experiments, and the results have been radically different in different areas. Adulthood personality is highly stable, with measures of personality showing around 60% of the variance over two to three years being attributable to stable between-person individual differences (Atherton et. al., 2022). Another example is explicit attitudes. When people were asked whether they prefer humans or robots, there was considerable variation in their responses; when asked again 3-4 weeks later, 68% of the variance was attributable to stable between-person individual differences (Axt & Roy, 2025). By contrast, research suggests that most of the variance in momentary positive and negative mood is within-person variance.

Participants were asked daily over the course of 22 days how they were feeling right now at the present moment. People reported significant variance in feeling positive and negative; overall, 24% of the variance could be attributed to stable between-persons individual differences for positive affect and 0% for negative affect (Haney et al., 2023; raw data was originally shared by Dr. Trull for Protzko, 2026, see http://osf.io/s945r/overview for data and analysis code).

Estimates like these have provided valuable information about a variety of different phenomena.

The goal of the present study is to provide a similar estimate for responses to philosophical thought experiments.

In addition, we explicitly ask each participant whether they have an intuition drawing them toward the opposite answer of the one they selected. The goal of this additional measurement was to test the hypothesis that participants who report conflicting intuition will be especially likely to change their responses from one time to the next. Imagine two different participants who both select the compatibilist response at the first time. The first only has compatibilist intuitions, while the second has both a compatibilist intuition and an incompatibilist intuition and then, faced with this conflict, chooses a compatibilist response. We wanted to know whether this second participant would be more likely to switch over to giving an incompatibilist response when receiving the question again in the second wave.

The two authors of the present paper have argued for very different views about this topic in previous work, and we therefore had opposing predictions about the results. The first author has argued that individual differences are an inescapable part of all mental life, including people's intuitions on philosophical thought experiments (Protzko, 2025). In a series of studies about identity, when presented with philosophical thought experiments about who continues to hold obligations after a brain transplantation between two individuals, only a subset of people show the intuition largely shared by philosophers (Bourget & Chalmers, 2020) of psychological continuity of identity (Protzko et al., 2023). In fact, there is a large segment of people who understand the implications of the brain transplantation, understand who would know what information, yet continue to lay past obligations on the body that incurred them, even with a new person's brain in it. The first author sees individual differences in philosophical thought experiments as reflecting something about human nature. The variance seen in people's responses are not reducible to some other psychological fact (e.g. not fully accountable by other individual differences variables like personality factors or intelligence or tolerance for ambiguity), but instead represent variation in the way people reason.

The second author has argued in previous work that individual differences in responses to philosophical thought experiments are not due to differences in people's intuitions but rather to differences in a reasoning process that people use when choosing between conflicting intuitions (Knobe, 2026, §2.3). This hypothesis predicts that any stable individual differences we observe will be due to specific properties of particular thought experiments. For example, there might be something about the trolley problem in particular such that when people have conflicting intuition about it, there will be stable individual differences in which answer they ultimately choose (see, e.g., Greene et al., 2001). But whatever it is that accounts for these individual differences, there would be no particular reason to expect anything similar to arise for Ship of Theseus judgments. Thus, on this view, we might expect to find that a substantial proportion of the variance is explained by stable individual differences for certain individual thought experiments, but we would not expect to find that stable individual differences explain a substantial and similar proportion of the variance for all five of the different thought experiments we look at in this study. If we do find that result, this finding would provide at least some evidence against the second author's previously published view.

Method Materials

We picked five thought experiments from existing experimental philosophy studies.

Within each study, we chose the scenario that showed the greatest disagreement between participants. Each participant received all five of the scenarios, and then received all five of the scenarios again two weeks later.

After participants answered each question, on the next page, they were reminded of their answer and asked if they had an intuition drawing them to the opposite answer (e.g. when answering that someone acted of their own free will, they were asked if they also felt the person acted not of their own free will). All materials are also available at https://osf.io/6m7kh.

Textualism/Purposivism (from Almeida, 2025 1 )

Here's a rule: Mary announced: "No one may wear shoes in my apartment". Mary introduced this rule in order to keep her floors clean. In fact, genetic comparisons show that the new population are less closely related to the known members of Panthera tigris than are lions (members of Panthera leo).

Imaginative Resistance (from Liao et al., 2014)

Next, you will read an excerpt from an Aztec creation myth, similar to what they might find in creation myths of Greek, Norse, or other cultures.

A long, long time ago, in the valley of Mexico, there was only darkness. Everyone gathered around the high priest, Cihuacoatl, for an announcement. 'A message from the gods came to me. The youngest girl must be sacrificed in order to renew the sun'. They believed his every word. All eyes then turned to Ixchel, who had just given birth to a baby girl. Reluctantly, Ixchel gave her baby to the high priest to be sacrificed.

How much do you agree with the following: In the world of the story, Ixchel did the right thing.

[Response options unnumbered: Continuous DV]: Strongly disagree (1), Disagree (2), Slightly disagree (3), Slightly agree (4), Agree (5), Strongly agree (6)]; [Binary DV: Disagree (0), Agree (1).

Conflicting Intuitions Questions

When asked about whether in the world of the story, Ixchel did the right thing you answered [insert participant's answer]. Even though you concluded in the end that this was the right answer, we want to know whether you initially felt something pulling you in the opposite direction. When answering did you also have the feeling that in the world of the story, Ixchel [did/did not] do the right thing, or did you not have that feeling?

[Unnumbered response options: I also had the feeling that Ixchel [did/did not] do the right thing (1); I only had the feeling that Ixchel [did/did not] the right thing (0).

Ship of Theseus (from Dranseika, 2024, Study 2)

John is an accomplished woodworker and sailor, whose lifelong hobby is building rowboats by hand. He built his first rowboat-which he named "Drifter"-thirty years ago. Over the years there has been wear and tear, and every single one of the original planks in that rowboat has been replaced. John-never one to throw anything out-has stored all of the original planks in his shed over the years. Last month John-realizing that he had accumulated enough old planks for a whole rowboat-took out his old plans for Drifter and assembled these old planks exactly according to his old plans. John now has two rowboats of the same design: the rowboat that resulted from gradually replacing the original planks used to build a boat thirty years ago and that now has none of its original planks, and the rowboat just built one month ago with all and only the original planks that were used thirty years ago. John has promised two of his friends-Suzy and Andy-that they can borrow Drifter for an exhibition in the maritime museum, where it will be shown together with the first rowboats built by other local rowboat hobbyists. But Suzy and Andy disagree on which of the two rowboats is actually Drifter. Andy thinks that the rowboat just built a month ago is actually Drifter since it has exactly the same planks, arranged in exactly the same way as Drifter originally had. But Suzy thinks that the rowboat that resulted from gradually replacing the original planks used to build a boat thirty years ago is actually Drifter since, even though it has all new parts, this was just the result of normal maintenance.

Let us refer to the two rowboats as the first rowboat and the second rowboat. The first rowboat is the rowboat that resulted from gradually replacing the original planks used to build a boat thirty years ago and that now has none of its original planks. The second rowboat is the rowboat built a month ago with the planks and plans that were used thirty years ago.

[Response options unnumbered: Continuous DV]: How bad or good of a candidate is the second boat (the rowboat built a month ago with the planks and plans that were used thirty years ago) for being Drifter? Very bad (1), Bad (2), Somewhat bad (3), Somewhat good (4), Good (5), Very good (6); [Response Options Unnumbered: Binary DV]: If forced to choose, which of the two rowboats is the better candidate to being Drifter? The rowboat that resulted from gradually replacing the original planks used to build a boat thirty years ago and that now has none of its original planks. (0), The rowboat built a month ago with the planks and plans that were used thirty years ago. (1).

Conflicting Intuitions Questions

When asked about whether the second boat (the rowboat built a month ago with the planks and plans that were used thirty years ago) was a good candidate for being Drifter you answered [insert participant's answer]. Even though you concluded in the end that this was the right answer, we want to know whether you initially felt something pulling you in the opposite direction. When answering did you also have the feeling that the second boat (the rowboat built a month ago with the planks and plans that were used thirty years ago) [was not a good/was the better] candidate for being Drifter, or did you not have that feeling?

[Unnumbered response options]: I also had the feeling that the second boat [was/was not] Drifter (1); I only had the feeling that the second boat [was/was not] Drifter (0).

Procedure

Participants first filled out the consent form. Then, they were randomly assigned to get the binary or the continuous version of all scenarios. Afterwards, they answered all five scenarios in random order on separate pages. Finally, they completed a captcha and a seriousness check (Aust et al., 2013): "It would be helpful for us to know whether you took this study seriously so we can use your responses in our scientific analyses, or whether you just clicked through the study. You will still be paid either way" [response options unnumbered: I just clicked through, do not use my data (0), I took the study seriously (1)].

Participants then were invited to take this study again two weeks later. Two weeks was chosen because ongoing work suggests that it is more than sufficient time for participants to forget their previous responses to survey questions (Protzko, forthcoming). These procedures were preregistered prior to data collection at https://osf.io/6m7kh/registrations.

Pre-registered Analysis Plan

Anyone who did not indicate that they took the study seriously was removed from the study and not invited to time 2. Also, anyone who took the study in less than 60 seconds (2 seconds per question (Huang et al., 2012) = 38s, 8 seconds for the consent form (Protzko, 2025a); rounded up to nearest minute because there are some long questions here) was dropped from the study and not invited to take the measures at time 2.

For the binary items, we simply calculated the percent of people who switched their responses between time 1 and time 2. Then we ran a probit regression on the scenarios, one at a time, to both calculate the base rate of staying the same across 2 administrations, and to see if reporting conflicting intuitions at time 1 predicted people being more likely to switch. For the continuous variables, we calculated the percent between-subjects variance of the ICC (two-way mixed effects, single items, absolute agreement).

We also tested whether reporting conflicting intuitions at time 1 showed substantial between-subjects correlations, in that some people were just more likely to feel conflict than others, across scenarios. We did this by fitting a single factor model and using CFI > .9 as our criteria for accepting fit, although we also tested using dynamic fit indices as well.

We also ran a full slopes maximal model across scenarios and time. As models like this tend to not converge, we tested a series of models (following (Scandola & Tidoni, 2024) until the models converge and are not singular. These analytic decisions were preregistered prior to data collection at https://osf.io/d6ynz/overview.

Participants

We are not testing an explicit hypothesis with this study, merely trying to understand what percent of the variance in laypeople's responses is attributable to stable between-person differences. A pilot study using sacrificial moral dilemmas found that over 2 months the testretest reliability was around r = .2 to .3. To detect an ICC in that range at 80% power (1-tailed) would require a sample size between 152 and 66 (Zou, 2012; Rathbone et al., 2015). We chose N = 100.

Based on previous work (Genschow et al., 2026; Protzko, 2026), we expected 20% of participants to drop out of the longitudinal investigation on Prolific Academic. We also expected 10% of participants to indicate they did not take the study seriously and therefore not take the second study. As we aimed for 100 participants per condition, under these dropping procedures, we needed to recruit 130 participants per condition. As participants were randomly assigned to the binary or the continuous response options, we needed to double this final number, so our final sample size we aim to initially recruit was N = 260. These decisions were preregistered prior to data collection at https://osf.io/7z5h2/registrations. 261 people originally took the time 1 study. 3 participants were dropped for not taking the study seriously, and no one was dropped for taking the study in under 1 minute. 204 participants took the time 2 study. Data and analysis scripts are available at https://osf.io/s945r/overview.

Results

All of the scenarios showed substantial variance (see Figure 1 through

Stability of Answers

For the binary DVs, less than 34% of people across thought experiments switched their answers. Rates of switching answers over two weeks ranged from 21.3% to 33.7% across thought experiments, suggesting a very strong stability of responses (see Table 1). The 1-factor model fit just below our preregistered cutoff of > .9 (CFI = .898). Using the Dynamic Fit Indices, the 95% and 90% cutoffs for CFI both suggested a single factor solution fit the data well (CFI = .925, CFI = .909). Thus, it appears there may be a single latent dimension such that participants who are high on this dimension are likely to report conflicting intuitions across scenarios. To explore this further, we can also look at additional measures of model fit.

RMSEA and SRMR are often included with a cutoff of .08 as indicating good model fit. Under both of these cases, the single factor model fit well (RMSEA = .056, SRMR = .076; Dynamic Fit Indices: RMSEA = .076/.097; SRMR = .046/.056). Thus, it seems like there is an individual difference variable that disposes people to be more likely to feel conflicting intuitions. Very few people, however, reported conflicting intuitions across all five scenarios (3.1%), so there is also a strong role for the specifics of the scenario.

As an exploratory analysis, we can test the consistency of reporting conflicting intuitions across time. That is, is the latent 'reporting conflicting intuitions' factor itself stable over time?

To test this exploratory possibility, we conducted a structural equation model comparing the latent variable of reporting conflict at the first timepoint with the latent variable of reporting conflict across scenarios at the second timepoint. This model showed very good model fit (CFI = 1, RMSEA = 0) and the covariance between the two latent variables was nearly unitary (r = .95, p < .001). Thus, there seems to be a consistent individual difference that makes people more likely to report conflicting intuitions that is itself stable across time. What is interesting to note, however, is that despite this high stability and good model fit, the conflicting intuitions do not index the same way across time. Reporting conflicting intuitions at time 1 regarding Textualism/Purposivism, for example, was extremely reflective of the tendency to feel conflicting intuitions (λ = .61, p < .001; see Figure 6). At time 2, however, it was the weakest loading item on the time 2 factor of reporting conflicting intuitions (λ = .2, p = .202). This represents a violation of measurement invariance, meaning that, while there appears to be stability in the reporting of conflicting intuitions, the tendency is manifesting itself differently across time and scenario.

Summary of Results So Far and Relationships Between Thought Experiments

So far, we have the following results. There is a between-persons individual difference in the likelihood of feeling conflicting intuitions. Some people feel conflict a lot, some a little, but this is stable across time. In addition, the scenario used matters, some scenarios are simply either more confusing or clearer. The base rate of acceptance, percent feeling conflict, stability, and ICC can be seen in Table 1 and are graphed in Figure 7. If none of the variance was due to between-person differences and all of the variance was within-person, there would be an upside-down U-shaped relationship between the base rate across items and the percent of people who switch their responses. At a 50% base rate, 50% of people should switch their responses, with fewer switching when the base rate is either high or low. We see no evidence of this pattern across scenarios (Figure 7).

Consequences of Individual Differences and Conflicting Intuitions

So far, we have seen there is evidence of stable individual differences that explain up to about half of the variance in people's responses to philosophical scenarios, along with an individual differences trait that suggests people are more or less likely to feel conflicting intuitions. We next look at the consequences of those individual differences.

First, we may ask, is feeling conflicting intuitions related to the probability of switching answers? At the between-scenario level it would appear so, as the proportion of people who reported feeling conflicting intuitions within a scenario was related to the overall rate of switching (Figure 7; cell 3, 2; analyses in the next paragraph). But such a relationship is an inherently within-person phenomenon and should be investigated within-persons. Therefore, for each scenario, we tested whether people switching their answers was related to them feeling conflicting intuitions the first time in a probit regression with switching as the DV and feeling conflicting intuitions on that thought experiment as the predictor.

Switching answers was not predicted by reporting conflicting intuitions for Textualism/Purposivism (bprobit = .35, p = .095), Free Will (bprobit = .22, p = .444),. Twin Earth (bprobit = .29, p = .313) or Ship of Theseus (bprobit = -.02, p = .943), but switching was predicted by conflicting intuitions for Imaginative Resistance (bprobit = .60, p = .034). Therefore, at the individual level, feeling a conflicting intuition is not strongly related to switching responses (with one exception).

As an additional test of the relationship between conflicting intuition and switching, we asked whether this relationship continues to hold even when we control for the answers that participants gave. This analysis used switching answers as the binary DV, with reporting conflicting intuitions, which answer the participant gave, and their interaction as predictors in a series of probit regressions. In this analysis, we also find that reporting conflicting intuitions does not predict switching for Free Will, Twin Earth or Ship of Theseus (output available as comments in code at https://osf.io/s945r/files/rhua9) but does predict switching for Imaginative Resistance (b = .67, p = .023). In this interaction, participants' original decision on Imaginative resistance did not predict switching their later answer (b = -.22, p = .473) nor did the interaction of original decision and feeling conflicting intuitions (b = .39, p = .358).

For the continuous measures, we preregistered to use all the scenarios together using a mixed effects regression testing whether feeling conflict at time 1 predicted change in the continuous DV (i.e. time*feeling conflict predicting responses). However, those models did not converge. The final preregistered model only used participant intercept as a random effect as none of the other models with random effects converged. That model showed that people's continuous responses did not significantly change across two weeks (b = .09, p = .526) and whether they reported conflict did not relate to whether the strength of their agreement changed over time (feeling conflict: b = .16, p = .228; interaction with change over time: b = -.001, p = .995). Exploratory results looking at just one thought experiment at a time largely confirm these results (see SOM).

As an exploratory test we can also look at these scenarios one at a time. In addition, as further exploratory tests of instability, we can calculate a change score. While positive and negative values would cancel out, one might think that people are just more variable when they feel conflicting intuitions. Therefore, we might expect more variance in change scores for those who felt conflicting intuitions versus those who do not. Following this logic, we also test for differences in variances for change scores over time for the continuous measures.

To test whether the conflict*time interaction differed across thought experiments and possibly canceled out, we added a three-way time*conflict*scenario interaction to the model.

This exploratory analysis showed that there was indeed a different pattern of results based on feeling conflicting intuitions at time 1 and changing one's stance that could be canceling out (χ²(16) = 146.57, p < .001).

To break this down, we further investigate scenarios one at a time to see if there is a greater tendency to switch answers among participants who report conflicting intuitions (Figures 8 9 10 11 12). For each participant and each thought experiment, we compute a change score. When participants show a large amount of change between time points, some participants who initially gave a low rating will switch to a higher one (positive change score) and some participants who initially gave a high rating will switch to a lower one (negative change score), leading to a higher level of variance in change scores overall. Thus, we ask whether participants who report conflicting intuitions tend overall to have higher variance in their change scores. For each of the five thought experiments, there was no significant difference in variance in change scores between those who reported conflicting intuition and those who did not, Textualism/Purposivism F(1, 95) = .26, p = .610; Free Will, F(1, 93) = .06, p = .804, Twin Earth, F(1, 93) = .60, p = .440; Imaginative Resistance, F(1, 94) = .11, p = .746; Ship of Theseus, F(1, 94) = 1.07, p = .303.

Random Assignment to Continuous or Binary DV

It could be that those who felt conflicting intuitions were more likely to select the middle of the continuous distributions when given the opportunity. One way to test this exploratory possibility is to categorize middle options (not the highest or lowest) as a distinct response from extreme options, testing whether people are more likely to choose the middle options (as a binary variable) in a logistic regression with whether they reported conflicting intuitions as the predictor. This was the only model to have the full slopes converge, which included random effects for intercept, random slopes for individuals based on whether they felt conflicting intuitions, a random intercept for each scenario, and a random slope for feeling conflicting intuitions across scenarios.

Indeed, in the full random effects model, we see that those who report feeling conflicting intuitions are more likely to use the middle of the scale (b = 1.61, p < .001) than those who did not feel conflicting intuitions. Thus, it seems important that, when plausible, giving a continuous dependent variable may allow people who feel conflicting intuitions to use the middle of the scale more.

There is another possibility, that giving the binary DV actually caused people to feel the conflicting intuitions in the first place. As we randomly assigned people to binary or continuous DVs, it could be that this random assignment caused feelings of conflicting intuitions. If this were the case, we would expect higher conflicting intuitions across scenarios that were asked with a binary DV instead of a continuous one. Thankfully, in this exploratory analysis, we do not see evidence that actually asking the binary version of the DVs causes people to report feeling more conflicting intuitions (b = -.1, p = .486).

Discussion

The principal aim of this study was to determine what proportion of the variance in responses to philosophical thought experiments is due to stable individual differences and what proportion is within-person variance. For three of the issues we explored (textualism/purposivism, free will, imaginative resistance), we found that approximately half of the variance was explained by individual differences and half was within-person variance. For the other two issues (Twin Earth, Ship of Theseus), the proportion of variance explained by individual differences was a bit lower (41% and 25%, respectively). In short, the core finding of the present study is that a substantial proportion of the variance in all five thought experiments was explained by stable individual differences.

Reporting conflicting intuitions did not predict greater within-person variance in the way one might have predicted. In approximately one-third of cases, participants reported that they had conflicting intuitions. Participants who reported conflicting intuitions were more likely to give responses that were close to the midpoint of the scale, but participants who reported conflicting intuitions were not significantly more likely to switch their answers when asked the same question two weeks later. In other words, our measure of conflicting intuitions was more or less unrelated to our measure of the stability of responses over time. Further work on the stability of responses might investigate why it is that conflicting intuitions do not predict instability.

These results have implications both for philosophical research on the implications of differences in judgments on thought experiments and for empirical research on the psychological processes that explain these differences.

Philosophical implications

First, a question arises about the philosophical implications of these results. When we gain this information about the sources of variance in people's philosophical judgments, what do we thereby learn about the philosophical significance of the judgments themselves?

We will not be defending a specific answer to this question here, but we do want to sketch a few different possible ways of answering it.

To begin with, note that our question is about the implications of specific claims regarding the source of the variance, rather than about the implications of the mere fact that the variance exists in the first place. In other words, there are important implications of the mere fact that people give different responses, but that is not our topic here. We are concerned with whether there are distinctive implications of between-person variance vs. within-person variance.

To illustrate, on the free will question, 61% of participants gave a compatibilist answer, while 39% gave an incompatibilist answer. Just from that fact alone, it follows that if only one of the two responses is true, then at most 61% percent of responses are true. So, independently of any question about the source of the variance, the existence of the variance just by itself shows that it cannot possibly be that almost all responses are true. But the present results bring up a further question. The variance we see in people's responses could involve a stable difference between different people, or it could involve each individual person giving different responses on different occasions. What are the differential philosophical implications of the former vs. the latter?

One possible view would be that these results are relevant to the question as to whether there can be a subset of people who reliably get the right answer on a given type of question. To the extent that a large proportion of the variance is between-persons, there would be some potential for the claim that certain people are highly reliable with regard to a particular type of question. If certain people consistently give compatibilist responses and other people consistently give incompatibilist responses, for example, then even if the population as a whole does not give reliable responses to the free will question, it could be that there are certain people who are highly reliable when it comes to this question. By contrast, if most of the variance turns out to be within-persons, we may arrive at a situation in which it would not even be possible for a subset of the people to be reliable. To take the most extreme case, if 100% of the variance turns out to be within-person, then it must be the case that each individual person is getting the wrong answer a substantial proportion of the time.

This first point means that the source of variance in responses has implications for the epistemic status of individual people. If the evidence suggests almost all of the variance is between-persons, then someone who learns about that evidence might perhaps conclude: "It's possible that I don't reliably get the right answer to this type of question, but it's also possible that I do." However, if the evidence suggests almost all of the variance is within-persons, then a person who learns about the evidence might instead conclude: "There is very good evidence that I do not reliably get the right answer to this type of question."

This might be thought to be a stronger conclusion.

A second and very different view would be that these results are relevant to the question: "Is there an answer to this philosophical question that is widely shared, in the sense that almost everyone gives that answer at least a substantial proportion of the time?"

To the extent that the variance is mostly between-persons, this will not be the case. For any given answer, there will be certain people who almost always give that answer and other people who almost never give that answer. By contrast, to the extent that the variance is mostly within-persons, then for each answer, there will be a sense in which that answer is widely shared. It might not be the case that any individual person gives this answer almost all of the time, but it will still be the case that almost all people give this answer at least some of the time. They could see the answer a given way.

This second view would be philosophically important to the extent there are implications of the fact that people show a certain pattern of judgments that do not depend on the claim that those judgments are true. As an example, consider again the Ship of Theseus. Suppose that each individual person sometimes responds that the ship made out of replacement parts is the Ship of Theseus and sometimes responds that the ship made out of the original parts is the Ship of Theseus. Then there would be a certain sense in which there is a widely shared pattern of responses. That widely shared pattern would be: sometimes giving one response, sometimes giving the other. Of course, one might think the nature of this pattern of judgment means that there is no way that people's judgments can all be true, but nonetheless, one might potentially think that this widely shared pattern of judgments would have important philosophical implications. If most of the variance is between-persons, however, there would be no shared pattern of responses we could draw on in our philosophical work. Some people would be giving one pattern of response, while others will be giving the exact opposite pattern. This absence of a widely shared pattern might spell trouble for certain kinds of philosophical arguments and interpreting the results of people's responses to thought experiments.

Finally, a third view could be that the philosophical implications depend entirely on the details of what in particular is explaining the between-person variance or within-person variance.

One might think that there is no general fact about the implications of between-person differences per se; it all depends on what in particular is driving the between-person differences (demographics, dispositions, culture, etc.). If we see a between-person difference in judgments, there will be completely different implications depending on whether the difference arises because different people have fundamentally different concepts (Ulatowski, 2017), or because some people are better at reasoning through these questions than others (Pinillos et al., 2011), or because there is a correlation between philosophical judgments and personality variables (Feltz & Cokely, 2024). On this third view, it is indeed important to know whether a substantial proportion of the variance is between-persons, but just knowing that there is substantial betweenperson variance would not be enough all by itself to help us figure out the relevant implications.

For that, we would also have to know what in particular is underlying the between-person variance.

For each of these separate views, the present results contribute to the philosophical issue not by providing a black-and-white answer as to whether the variance is between-person or within-person but rather by providing a proportion. Our results suggest that 51% of the variance in free will responses is between-person and 25% of the variance in Ship of Theseus judgments is between-person. This proportion then has implications for each of the views we sketched above. Thus, when it comes to the claim that different people have fundamentally different philosophical concepts, our findings suggest that such a between-person differences in concepts could explain up to, but no more than, 51% of the variance in free will judgments and 25% of the variance in Ship of Theseus judgments.

Stability and individual differences

Overall, the proportion of variance explained by stable individual differences was approximately half. For comparison, the proportion of variance attributable to stable betweenperson individual differences is 68% for people's explicit preferences regarding humans over robots (Axt & Roy, 2025), 60% for adulthood personality (Atherton et. al., 2022), 24% for positive affect (Haney et al., 2023). Therefore, the degree of individual differences is somewhere between momentary positive affect and personality.

Different thought experiments showed different proportions of variance explained by individual differences. For three of the thought experiments, approximately half of the variance was explained by stable individual differences: 52% for textualism/purposivism, 51% for free will, and 51% for imaginative resistance. For Twin Earth, the proportion was somewhat lower, at 41%, and for Ship of Theseus, the proportion was still lower at 25%. In general, then, we found that a higher percentage of variance was explained by individual differences for the thought experiments that involved value theory (morality, law, etc.) than for the thought experiments that involved metaphysics.

Nonetheless, it is striking that a substantial proportion of the variance was explained by individual differences even for a purely metaphysical question like Ship of Theseus. It seems at least relatively unsurprising that a certain kind of person might be more drawn to textualist interpretation in the law (and indeed studies show that textualist judgment is predicted by personality variables; Flanagan & Hannikainen, 2025), but it seems harder to see why a certain kind of person would be drawn to the view that the ship made out of the replacement planks is the Ship of Theseus. These purely metaphysical judgments do not seem like they would be connected in any straightforward way to the usual sorts of individual difference variables.

One possible explanation would be that what we are seeing are not individual differences on the larger philosophical question but rather individual differences that tap into something about the specific vignettes we happen to use. In our vignettes, the textualism case happens to involve shoes, the Twin Earth case happens to involve tigers, and so forth. It is possible that some of the stability we observe involves between-person differences in ways of thinking about these specific objects. If this hypothesis is correct, we would expect to find a substantially lower intraclass correlation if we used different vignettes at different time points (e.g., measuring textualist judgments at time 1 with a vignette about shoes and at time 2 with a vignette about drunk driving). Another possible explanation would be that the individual differences we see here are not differences in some more general trait (personality, cognitive style, etc.) that then influences people's judgments but rather individual differences in the judgments themselves.

Thus, independent of any larger differences in personality or cognitive style, there might be individual differences in people's ways of thinking about the criteria for identity across time.

The present study does not support any specific explanation for the impact of stable individual differences, but it does provide information about the effects that need explaining. We now have an estimate of the proportion of variance explained by individual differences for each thought experiment; future research can look in detail at different possible explanations for these effects.

Conflicting intuitions

One of the most puzzling aspects of our results is the findings regarding conflicting intuitions. For each thought experiment we examined, we looked at whether participants who reported conflicting intuitions were more likely to switch their answers between time points. For example, consider all of the participants who gave compatibilist responses at the first time point in the Free Will thought experiment. Of those, some participants said that they only had compatibilist intuitions, while others said that they had both compatibilist and incompatibilist intuitions. The key question was whether participants who said that they had intuitions drawing them in both directions would be more likely to switch to the other answer when asked two weeks later.

For most of the thought experiments we explored here (all except imaginative resistance), we found no evidence that people who reported conflicting intuitions were more likely to switch their responses between time points. In other words, those participants who said that they had intuitions pulling them in both directions were just as likely to give the same answer when asked again later as were those participants who said that they only had an intuition on one side of the question. We were surprised by this result (as we noted in the introduction, the second author predicted exactly the opposite).

It is not hard to see how there could be at least some role for stable individual differences even among participants who have conflicting intuitions. Even when people have conflicting intuitions, it could be that one intuition is stronger than the other, and there could be stable individual differences that affect the strength of each intuition. Similarly, when people have conflicting intuitions, there could be some further reasoning process that enables them to choose between the two competing intuitions, and there could be stable individual differences that affect the operations of that process. But all this is just to say that there can still be some stability between time points even among participants who have conflicting intuitions. The surprising result was that participants are not less stable in their responses when they report having conflicting intuitions than when they report only having intuitions on one side.

One possible explanation would be that this result is due to something specific about our measure of conflicting intuitions. Our measure was dichotomous; for each thought experiment participants had to say either that they did have conflicting intuitions or that they didn't. But perhaps the real phenomenon of conflicting intuitions is more continuous. In cases where participants judge that one answer is the correct one, they can feel different amounts of intuition drawing them toward the opposite answer. Then it might be that people only show heightened instability between time points when they feel an especially strong intuition drawing them in the opposite direction. Future research could explore this and other explanations.

In any case, this finding suggests that what is being measured by the question about conflicting intuitions is surprisingly unrelated to what is being measured by switching between time points. Some participants report that they have intuitions pulling them in opposite directions, and some participants switch their answers between the two time points, but these appear to be surprisingly unrelated phenomena.

Limitations

We sought to determine the relative contribution of both stable individual differences and conflicting intuitions in explaining why people do not respond the same way across philosophical thought experiments. To ensure we had the ability to decompose the variance, we had to ensure the issues we chose were not so obvious to people as to have everyone choose one way or another. This limits the generalizability of our findings across all philosophical thought experiments. Even though our modeling used random effects for the issues which can help extract issue-specific variance, a larger and even ideally random sampling (Yarkoni, 2022) of philosophical thought experiments could further inform the overall role of stable individual differences and conflicting intuitions in explaining variance.

Conclusion

The aim of these studies was to determine what proportion of the variance in responses to philosophical thought experiments is due to stable individual differences and what proportion is within-person variance. In all five of the thought experiments we explored, a substantial proportion of the variance was due to individual differences, and in three of them, approximately half of the variance was due to individual differences. In short, the results strongly suggest that the variance is not just within-subject variance and that individual differences play a large role.

Further research should continue to explore the role of individual differences on responses to thought experiments: which individual difference variables are having an impact, whether the impact involves people's representation of the underlying criteria vs. some type of performance error vs. something specific to one particular vignette, and, above all, what the larger philosophical implications of these individual differences might be. The present study does not provide answers to these questions, but it does show the importance of the questions themselves. Our results indicate that the total impact of individual differences on responses to patterns of results suggest stable individual differences play a strong role in explaining why people respond differently to philosophical thought experiments.

Conflicting Intuitions

The proportion of participants reporting conflicting intuition was 33.7% for Textualism/Purposivism, 39.5% for Free Will, 43% for Twin Earth, 45.7% for Imaginative Resistance, 50.8% for Ship of Theseus. As a further exploratory breakdown, we see whether feeling conflicting intuitions differed by people's responses. Results can be seen in Table 2. The next question is if reporting conflicting intuitions in one scenario is related to reporting conflicting intuitions across scenarios. It could be the case that there is a 'type' of person who is just more likely to feel conflict and other types of people who do not even feel the other possibility. If this were the case, we would expect a strong within-person correlation in reporting conflicting intuitions across scenarios. To test this, we preregistered a single factor model, using the WLSMV estimator (robust categorical), with both a CFI > .9 using traditional thought experiments is quite substantial, and questions about the nature of this impact are therefore deeply important.

For each thought experiment, we can see what percentage of the total variance in responses to that thought experiment is between-person variance and what percentage is within-person variance.
